title: Getting the call and Duke's trailer in Boston
summary: Mercer Ellington needs a trombonist for two Sundays; Baron takes his seat on the bus and Duke invites him to stay in a backstage trailer scene in Boston.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: I was going mouth him. So Mercer was managing the band at the time, called Jimmy and said, “We need a trombone player for two Sundays.” And Jimmy recommended me. I got the call for that gig. I remember being, right around then I was out at my mom’s house with someone else and I just pulled out a record I said, “This is who I’m playing with next week.” I was like — and I remember calling people and the big advice I got, not from Jimmy, from someone else said, “Make sure you don’t sit in someone’s seat on the bus.” And I go like, “Well how do I know?” So I get on the bus and I heard this booming voice, “You sit here, boy.” That’s where I sat forever since then. Third one on the right, that’s my home. Chuck Connors in front of me, Russell Procope to the right. And so I had those two gigs, and I figured well, that’ll be on my resume, two gigs with Duke Ellington. So on the second one, it was a big outdoor concert in Boston. I forgot where it was but a woman named Elma Lewis has this whole, I don’t know if she’s still around but she had this whole thing for the community all over the place. I think it was a free concert. A big outdoor thing. So we’re setting up and Duke says, “You want to come out with us, you want to play with us.” And then you know, he says, “Just come in my trailer afterwards.” He had a trailer. And I was like — whoa. I though it was like two gigs. So I’m in the trailer and it’s a little bigger than an average dressing room trailer for one. The place is packed with people. Food, caviar, ice cream, all kinds of drinks, booze, everything. He says, “Artie, just have a drink, have some food, I’ll be right back.” “Oh Duke,” and Duke goes out to talk to this woman, and he comes back twenty minutes later and says, “So Artie, you want to come out and play with us?” “Oh yeah, man, I’d love to.” He says, “Well let’s talk about detai—” “Oh Duke, come here for a minute please, Duke.” And when he heard the woman’s voice he had to go like. It was like that for about 45 minutes. So next time he comes back he says, “Artie, here’s my phone number, we won’t be able © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

to talk business here, but call me tomorrow or something.” I was like, some friends of mine who lived in Boston, I was staying with them, I was like whoa, I was like blown away. Then I talked to him a day or two later and so I’m on the phone and he says, “Well how much do you want?” Oh, no, actually, we didn’t even talk money. He just said, “Well we’re leaving ten days from now, and then in a month we’re going to Europe, we’re going to Africa for about five or six weeks.” I was like ohh, this is amazing. Then when we finally got on the road and there was room, he said, “Well how much do you want?” I’m like uh uh — how much do I have to pay.
Yeah, right. Oh you mean I get paid too?
So it was amazing. And you know Jimmy Maxwell, you know, my hero.
